title: Indicators are evidence

blocks.heading: Indicators are evidence
blocks.text: An indicator is a measurable feature used as evidence about a wider condition; one indicator seldom gives a complete account of development. An environmental measure describes environmental conditions; a social measure describes people's living conditions; a political measure concerns participation or rights; an economic measure concerns productive resources, output or income. Check the definition, date, unit and population before comparing values. A percentage and a total answer different questions. Two measures can move together without one being proven to cause the other.

blocks.heading: Environmental evidence
blocks.text: Environmental indicators include the share of households using safe water, a measure of air pollution or an area of forest lost. Interpret the direction: more safe-water access is generally an improvement, while more harmful pollution is deterioration. In a fictional settlement, comparable annual records show safe-water access rising from 55% to 75% and unsafe water samples falling from 18 to 6 out of 30 tested. Access improves by 20 percentage points, and unsafe samples fall by 12. Together the observations support an improvement in water-related environmental conditions. They do not describe the settlement's air quality or identify the cause of the changes.

blocks.heading: Social evidence
blocks.text: Social indicators include education, health, housing and service access. Literacy concerns the ability to read and write according to the measure used. Life expectancy is the average number of years a person at a stated age is expected to live under the mortality conditions used in the estimate; it is not a promise for an individual. Infant mortality rate records deaths before the first birthday per thousand live births for a stated period. In fictional District C, school participation rises from 70% to 85% and infant mortality falls from 40 to 25 per thousand live births. The combination supports improvement in education access and infant survival. Keep the units distinct: 15 percentage points and 15 deaths per thousand live births are not the same measure.

blocks.heading: Political evidence
blocks.text: Political development concerns opportunities to participate and influence decisions, rights and accountability. Indicators may include participation in a decision process or evidence of access to it. In an invented community election with 1,000 eligible adults in each period, participation rises from 400 to 700 adults, while the number of neighbourhoods able to use an accessible meeting venue rises from two of five to five of five. Wider access accompanies higher participation. Counts from a meeting alone would not establish that rights are protected or that everyone had a free choice. Identify what the source actually measures and combine complementary observations rather than treating one statistic as a complete political judgement.

blocks.heading: Economic evidence
blocks.text: Economic indicators can include income per person and employment. In fictional areas D and E, annual income per person is N$30,000 and N$45,000 respectively; employment among a consistently defined working-age population is 50% and 65%. E combines N$15,000 more average income with employment 15 percentage points higher. This supports a stronger position on those two measures. It does not show how much the lowest-income households receive or the quality of available jobs. Comparable definitions matter: changing the age range or what counts as employment can change the apparent pattern.

blocks.heading: National totals and per-person figures
blocks.text: A national total is the amount for the whole country. A per-person figure divides a total by population. GNP of N$120 million shared across 6,000 people gives N$20,000 per person for that period. A learner who calls the N$20,000 figure the national total has confused the two measures. GNI per person is also an average, rather than the income received by the whole nation. The separating test is whether the national measure has been divided by population. Neither average means that each person actually receives that amount. These examples explain the total-versus-average distinction, without treating different national accounting labels as interchangeable in every dataset.

blocks.heading: Combine dimensions without hiding a conflict
blocks.text: Two fictional areas each have annual income per person of N$40,000. Area F has 90% safe-water access and a 20-minute average journey to a clinic; Area G has 50% access and an 80-minute journey. The equal income averages conceal differences in environmental and social access. Area F has water access 40 percentage points higher and a clinic journey 60 minutes shorter. Those differences justify examining service access separately from income. They do not prove that Area F is better on every aspect of development, since the data says nothing about participation or income distribution.

blocks.heading: Choose the measure for the question
blocks.text: Health in Topic 7.2 and education in Topic 7.3 explain mechanisms behind social indicators. Research in Topic 10.1 explains how data is collected and assessed. To interpret a source, name the measured dimension, compare relevant observations with their units, and state the relationship they support. Add a limitation when the question needs a wider judgement, rather than allowing a caution to replace the required description.
